Comparing networks with compare_networks()

Mohammed Saqr

University of Eastern Finland

Sonsoles López-Pernas

University of Eastern Finland

Kamila Misiejuk

FernUniversität in Hagen, Germany
Source: vignettes/articles/compare-networks.Rmd
compare-networks.Rmd

Do two groups, or two periods, produce different networks? compare_networks() in Nestimate (Saqr, López-Pernas, & Misiejuk, 2026) compares two or more networks edge by edge, node by node and on global metrics, and returns one object from which every table and plot is drawn. By default the comparison is descriptive; test adds a permutation test, a Bayesian comparison or a bootstrap of the network structure.

Table Verb
One row per pair of networks summary()
One row per pair and edge edge_differences()
One row per pair, node and centrality measure node_differences()
One row per pair and global metric global_differences()
One row per network and structural metric network_metrics()

Data

group_regulation_long records the regulation actions of 2,000 students working in 200 teams of 10, generated synthetically from the group_regulation data of the tna package (Tikka, López-Pernas, & Saqr, 2025). Achievement (Achiever, High or Low) is recorded per team. build_network() with group = "Achiever" estimates one transition network per level.

library(Nestimate)
achievers <- build_network(group_regulation_long, method = "relative",
                           actor = "Actor", action = "Action",
                           time = "Time", group = "Achiever")
achievers
## Group Networks (2 groups, group_col: Achiever)
## 
##   Group  Nodes  Edges  Weights
##   High   9      76     [0.001, 0.576]
##   Low    9      75     [0.000, 0.462]

Describing the difference 

comparison <- compare_networks(achievers)
comparison
## Network comparison (descriptive): 2 networks, 1 pairs, scaling = none
##   networks: High (9 nodes, directed), Low (9 nodes, directed)
## 
##  pair        pearson mean|diff| max|diff| largest change                    
##  High vs Low 0.92    0.03       0.21      discuss -> consensus (High higher)
## 
## Tables: summary(x), edge_differences(x), node_differences(x), global_differences(x), network_metrics(x). Plot: plot(x, type = ...)
summary(comparison)
##         pair network_a network_b n_cells n_differing share_higher_a
##  High vs Low      High       Low      81          78           0.51
##  share_higher_b mean_abs_diff max_abs_diff pearson spearman cosine jaccard
##            0.46          0.03         0.21    0.92     0.92   0.95    0.75
##              top_edge top_edge_higher
##  discuss -> consensus            High

The comparison takes the difference High minus Low for each of the 81 cells of the weight matrices, self-loops included. 78 cells differ; High is higher in 51% of them and Low in 46%. The mean absolute difference is 0.03 and the largest, discuss to consensus, 0.21. The two networks are alike overall: the edge weights correlate at 0.92 (Pearson and Spearman), the cosine similarity is 0.95, and the Jaccard similarity of the edges present in each network is 0.75.

global_differences() reports 22 metrics in five groups: deviations of the weights (mean, median, root mean square and largest absolute difference), correlations, dissimilarities (Euclidean, Manhattan, Canberra, Bray-Curtis, Frobenius), similarities (cosine, Jaccard, Dice, overlap and the RV coefficient, a correlation between matrices; Robert & Escoufier, 1976), and the agreement of the ranks and signs of the weights.

plot(comparison, type = "global")

Each panel is one group of metrics, with a dotted line at the value of identical networks: 1 for correlations and similarities, 0 for deviations and dissimilarities.

network_metrics() describes each network on its own. Both are almost complete (76 and 75 of 81 possible edges, density 1 rounded), and their in-strengths are spread more widely in High (SD 0.91) than in Low (0.72).

edge_differences() gives one row per cell: the two weights, their difference, its absolute value, the relative difference (|a - b| / (|a| + |b|)), the ratio, the ranks of the edge in each network, status (present in both networks, in one, or in neither) and higher, the network in which the edge is larger. adapt to coregulate exists only in Low (0 against 0.03).

plot(comparison, type = "edges")

The edge view draws the 20 largest differences as a line between the two weights, a diamond for High and a square for Low. The line is solid blue where High is higher and dashed red where Low is higher, and is labelled with the difference. discuss to consensus (0.42 in High, 0.21 in Low) and synthesis to consensus (0.58 against 0.39) are the largest differences in favour of High, and synthesis to adapt (0.14 against 0.30) in favour of Low.

plot(comparison, type = "networks")

plot(comparison, type = "difference")

The networks view draws each network once; the difference view draws the signed difference network, blue for transitions stronger in High and red for transitions stronger in Low.

plot(comparison, type = "heatmap")

plot(comparison, type = "scatter")

The heatmap prints every cell of the difference matrix. The scatter plot sets each transition’s weight in High against its weight in Low; points on the diagonal are equal in both.

node_differences() compares the centralities of each state, by default in-strength, out-strength and betweenness. consensus receives the most in both networks, more in High (2.95 against 2.42), and adapt and coregulate receive more in Low.

plot(comparison, type = "nodes")

Permutation test

The descriptive tables show where the networks differ, not whether a difference is larger than sampling would produce. test = "permutation" reassigns the sequences to the two groups 1,000 times, re-estimates both networks each time, and compares the observed difference of each edge and node measure with the reassigned ones (Saqr et al., 2025). Two global statistics test whether the networks differ at all: M, the sum of the absolute differences over all cells, and S, the largest.

tested <- compare_networks(achievers, test = "permutation", iter = 1000,
                           seed = 1)
summary(tested)
##         pair network_a network_b n_cells n_differing share_higher_a
##  High vs Low      High       Low      81          78           0.51
##  share_higher_b mean_abs_diff max_abs_diff pearson spearman cosine jaccard
##            0.46          0.03         0.21    0.92     0.92   0.95    0.75
##              top_edge top_edge_higher n_sig_edges n_sig_nodes m_stat   m_p
##  discuss -> consensus            High          42          16   2.61 0.001
##  s_stat   s_p
##    0.21 0.001

42 of the 78 transitions and 16 of the 27 node measures differ at the 5% level, and both global statistics are significant (M = 2.61, S = 0.21, p = 0.001, the smallest p-value 1,000 permutations can give). adjust corrects the edge p-values for multiple testing, for example adjust = "BH".

plot(tested, type = "inference")

The inference view draws each edge difference as a bar from zero, with its p-value on the right; a filled marker is significant at 0.05.

Differences in centralities

measures = "all" compares nine centralities. In- and out-strength are the sums of a state’s incoming and outgoing transition probabilities (Opsahl, Agneessens, & Skvoretz, 2010). Closeness is the inverse of the summed shortest-path distances to a state (ClosenessIn), from it (ClosenessOut) or ignoring direction (Closeness), and betweenness the number of shortest paths that pass through it (Freeman, 1978); a heavier edge is a shorter step. BetweennessRSP counts randomised shortest paths, which include routes slightly longer than the shortest (Kivimäki et al., 2016). Diffusion sums the weights of the walks of up to n steps that start at a state (Banerjee et al., 2013), and Clustering is the weighted clustering coefficient (Onnela et al., 2005). The permutation test gives each a p-value.

centralities <- compare_networks(achievers, measures = "all",
                                 test = "permutation", iter = 1000, seed = 1)
summary(centralities)
##         pair network_a network_b n_cells n_differing share_higher_a
##  High vs Low      High       Low      81          78           0.51
##  share_higher_b mean_abs_diff max_abs_diff pearson spearman cosine jaccard
##            0.46          0.03         0.21    0.92     0.92   0.95    0.75
##              top_edge top_edge_higher n_sig_edges n_sig_nodes m_stat   m_p
##  discuss -> consensus            High          42          55   2.61 0.001
##  s_stat   s_p
##    0.21 0.001

55 of the 81 node measures (nine states, nine measures) differ at the 5% level: all nine closeness values, eight each for randomised-shortest-path betweenness and clustering, seven each for in-strength and in-closeness, five each for out-strength and diffusion, four for betweenness and two for out-closeness.

node_differences(centralities, measure = "Betweenness")

consensus lies on most shortest paths in both networks, more in High (30 against 25, p = 0.001). synthesis lies on 7 shortest paths in High and none in Low (p = 0.003), and emotion on 5 against 3 (p = 0.001); adapt lies on more in Low (4 against 1, p = 0.001). coregulate, discuss and plan differ by 2 or 3 paths without significance.

plot(centralities, type = "nodes",
     measure = c("Betweenness", "BetweennessRSP", "Closeness", "Diffusion"))

Edge betweenness

Betweenness can also be computed for edges: the number of shortest paths between states that pass through an edge (Girvan & Newman, 2002). An edge with a high value carries many of the routes through the network. net_edge_betweenness() returns one network per group whose weights are these counts, and permutation() tests the difference of every edge: it reassigns the sequences between the groups, re-estimates both transition networks and recomputes their edge betweenness each time.

edge_betweenness <- net_edge_betweenness(achievers)
edge_betweenness
## Group Networks (2 groups)
## 
##   Group  Nodes  Edges  Weights
##   High   9      24     [1.000, 15.000]
##   Low    9      29     [1.000, 14.000]
routes <- permutation(edge_betweenness, iter = 1000, seed = 1)
routes
## Grouped Permutation Test
## Groups: High vs Low 
## 
## -- High vs Low --
## Permutation Test: Edge-Betweenness Network [directed]
##   Iterations: 1000  |  Alpha: 0.05
##   Nodes: 9  |  Edges tested: 29  |  Significant: 10
subset(summary(routes), sig)
##          group       from         to weight_x weight_y diff effect_size
## 1  High vs Low      adapt   cohesion        2        4   -2  -44.766148
## 4  High vs Low   cohesion  consensus        7        3    4   14.910848
## 5  High vs Low   cohesion coregulate        0        4   -4  -14.910848
## 8  High vs Low  consensus    discuss       15       12    3   11.959977
## 11 High vs Low coregulate    discuss        4        6   -2   -5.064736
## 15 High vs Low    discuss      adapt        0        9   -9  -28.749445
## 16 High vs Low    discuss  consensus        7        4    3    3.062634
## 18 High vs Low    discuss  synthesis       15        8    7   22.360680
## 19 High vs Low    emotion   cohesion        6        4    2   13.801640
## 28 High vs Low  synthesis      adapt        9        3    6   10.341155
##        p_value  sig
## 1  0.000999001 TRUE
## 4  0.000999001 TRUE

## 11 0.000999001 TRUE

Shortest paths run over 24 edges in High and 29 in Low, and 10 of the 29 edges tested differ in the number of paths they carry. In Low, 9 shortest paths pass through discuss to adapt and none in High; in High, discuss to synthesis carries 15 against 8 and synthesis to adapt 9 against 3.

library(cograph)
splot(routes, edge_positive_color = "#4A6FE3",
      edge_negative_color = "#D33F6A")

cograph draws the edges that differ, blue where High carries more paths and red where Low does.

bayes_compare() is the Bayesian route. Edge betweenness is not a simple function of single transition probabilities, so it draws whole transition matrices from the Dirichlet posterior of each network, with the Jeffreys prior added to the counts, and recomputes edge betweenness on every one of 10,000 draws. diff is the posterior mean difference in the number of shortest paths, with its 95% credible interval; an edge is credibly different when the interval excludes zero.

routes_posterior <- bayes_compare(edge_betweenness, seed = 1)
routes_posterior
## Grouped Bayesian Dirichlet-Multinomial Comparison
## Comparisons: High vs Low 
## Use summary() for combined edge-level results.
head(summary(routes_posterior), 8)
##    comparison     from         to weight_x weight_y count_x count_y    diff
## 1 High vs Low    adapt   cohesion   1.9321   3.3765      37     102 -1.4444
## 2 High vs Low    adapt  consensus   6.0050   5.9339      73     170  0.0711
## 3 High vs Low    adapt coregulate   0.0000   0.0000       0      11  0.0000
## 4 High vs Low    adapt    discuss   0.0000   0.0166       5      25 -0.0166
## 5 High vs Low    adapt    emotion   0.9406   1.5377      20      41 -0.5971
## 6 High vs Low    adapt    monitor   0.0553   0.0341       4      13  0.0212
## 7 High vs Low    adapt       plan   0.0000   0.0000       2       6  0.0000
## 8 High vs Low cohesion      adapt   0.0000   0.0000       5       0  0.0000
##   effect_size ci_lower ci_upper ci_width p_difference p_value   sig
## 1 -2.00628791       -3        0        3       0.9999  0.0002 FALSE
## 2  0.16049834       -1        1        2       0.8894  0.2212 FALSE
## 3  0.00000000        0        0        0       1.0000  0.0000 FALSE
## 4 -0.09148479        0        0        0       1.0000  0.0000 FALSE
## 5 -0.98620607       -2        1        3       0.9713  0.0574 FALSE
## 6  0.06894516       -1        1        2       0.9472  0.1056 FALSE
## 7  0.00000000        0        0        0       1.0000  0.0000 FALSE
## 8  0.00000000        0        0        0       1.0000  0.0000 FALSE

2 of the 78 edges are credibly different: discuss to consensus carries 2.9 more shortest paths in High (95% interval 1 to 4), and coregulate to consensus carries one path in Low and almost none in High. Betweenness counts whole paths, so its posterior intervals run between whole numbers and are wide. discuss to adapt, which carries 7.1 paths in Low and none in High on average, has an interval from −9 to 0: every draw has it lower in High (p_difference = 1), but the interval reaches zero, so it is not credibly different. The permutation test found 10 edges, the Bayesian comparison 2; the two answer the question in different ways, by reassigning whole sequences and by drawing transition probabilities independently.

plot(routes_posterior)

Bayesian comparison

test = "bayes" models the transitions out of each state with a Dirichlet posterior in each network, with the Jeffreys prior of 0.5 added to every count (Jeffreys, 1946; Johnston & Jendoubi, 2026), and draws the difference of every edge from the two posteriors (Gelman et al., 2013). It reports the posterior mean difference, its 95% credible interval and the probability of direction, the posterior probability that the difference has the sign of its mean (Makowski et al., 2019). bayes_p is 2 * (1 - pd), a two-sided p-value equivalent.

bayesian <- compare_networks(achievers, test = "bayes", iter = 1000,
                             seed = 1)
summary(bayesian)
##         pair network_a network_b n_cells n_differing share_higher_a
##  High vs Low      High       Low      81          78           0.51
##  share_higher_b mean_abs_diff max_abs_diff pearson spearman cosine jaccard
##            0.46          0.03         0.21    0.92     0.92   0.95    0.75
##              top_edge top_edge_higher n_sig_edges
##  discuss -> consensus            High          39

39 transitions have a 95% credible interval that excludes zero, against 42 significant in the permutation test; the two agree on 76 of the 81 cells. The posterior treats the transitions as independent counts, while the permutation test reassigns whole sequences.

plot(bayesian, type = "inference")

Practical equivalence

A credible interval that excludes zero says the difference is not zero, not that it is large enough to matter. rope sets a region of practical equivalence around zero on the difference scale (Kruschke, 2018); here a difference of up to 0.02 in a transition probability is treated as negligible. Each edge is classed as different when its 95% credible interval lies entirely outside the region, equivalent when it lies entirely inside, and undecided otherwise.

equivalence <- compare_networks(achievers, test = "bayes", iter = 1000,
                                seed = 1, rope = 0.02)
subset(edge_differences(equivalence), bayes_decision == "different")

19 transitions are different, 22 practically equivalent and 40 undecided. The different ones include the largest differences of the descriptive comparison, such as discuss to consensus and synthesis to adapt.

bayes_compare()

bayes_compare() runs the same model on its own, with 10,000 posterior draws by default. An edge is credibly different when its 95% interval excludes zero, its posterior mean difference exceeds 0.01 in absolute value, and the interval bound nearest zero exceeds 0.001.

posterior <- bayes_compare(achievers, seed = 1)
head(summary(posterior), 8)
##    comparison     from         to    weight_x     weight_y count_x count_y
## 1 High vs Low    adapt   cohesion 0.257731959 0.2751677852      37     102
## 2 High vs Low    adapt  consensus 0.505154639 0.4577181208      73     170

## 8 High vs Low cohesion      adapt 0.005835544 0.0006565988       5       0

The table gives each transition’s weight and count in both networks, the posterior mean difference, an effect size (the difference divided by its posterior standard deviation), the credible interval and the probability that the difference has the sign of its mean (p_difference). 38 transitions are credibly different. adapt to coregulate occurs 11 times in Low and never in High; its interval, [−0.049, −0.008], excludes zero.

plot(posterior)

The plot draws the credibly different transitions as a difference network, blue where High is higher and red where Low is higher, each edge labelled with its posterior mean difference and credible interval.

Bootstrap of the structure

test = "bootstrap" resamples the nodes of each network (Snijders & Borgatti, 1999; Davison & Hinkley, 1997) and compares four structural measures: density, mean weight, centralization and reciprocity. It reads only the weight matrices, so it also works for matrices without data.

structural <- compare_networks(achievers, test = "bootstrap", iter = 1000,
                               seed = 1)
subset(global_differences(structural), category == "Structure (bootstrap)")
##         pair network_a network_b              category         metric
##  High vs Low      High       Low Structure (bootstrap)        density
##  High vs Low      High       Low Structure (bootstrap)    mean_weight
##  High vs Low      High       Low Structure (bootstrap) centralization
##  High vs Low      High       Low Structure (bootstrap)    reciprocity
##                  key value boot_observed_a boot_observed_b boot_se
##         boot_density  0.01            0.96            0.94    0.06
##     boot_mean_weight     0            0.12            0.12    0.04
##  boot_centralization  0.07            0.59            0.52    0.19
##     boot_reciprocity -0.04            0.40            0.43    0.13
##  boot_ci_lower boot_ci_upper boot_z boot_p boot_sig
##          -0.10          0.13   0.23  0.816    FALSE
##          -0.08          0.08   0.01  0.992    FALSE
##          -0.30          0.44   0.40  0.693    FALSE
##          -0.29          0.22  -0.28  0.783    FALSE

None of the four measures differs (p between 0.69 and 0.99): the two networks have the same overall structure, and they differ in which transitions carry the weight.

Accounting for nesting

Students are nested in teams, and the achievement level is given per team. With actor = "Group", the permutation test reassigns whole teams instead of single students, and global_differences() gains three Nesting rows.

nested <- compare_networks(achievers, test = "permutation", iter = 1000,
                           seed = 1, actor = "Group")
subset(global_differences(nested, digits = 3),
       category %in% c("Global Test (permutation)", "Nesting"))
##         pair network_a network_b                  category
##  High vs Low      High       Low Global Test (permutation)
##  High vs Low      High       Low Global Test (permutation)
##  High vs Low      High       Low                   Nesting
##  High vs Low      High       Low                   Nesting
##  High vs Low      High       Low                   Nesting
##                         metric         key  value perm_p perm_sig
##  M (total absolute difference)      perm_M  2.612  0.001     TRUE
##                   S (max edge)      perm_S  0.210  0.001     TRUE
##                            ICC         icc -0.002     NA       NA
##          Design effect (edges)  deff_edges  1.027     NA       NA
##              Design effect (M) deff_global  1.201     NA       NA

The intraclass correlation is −0.002, and the design effect is 1.03 for the transitions and 1.20 for M. The networks still differ overall (M = 2.61, p = 0.001), and 42 transitions remain significant. The article on nested data describes these quantities.

More than two networks

mark_phases() divides each student’s actions into three phases of equal length, and build_network() estimates one network per phase. Every student contributes to all three phases, so with actor = "Actor" the permutation test reassigns each student’s sequences between phases within the student. reference = "early" compares the other two phases with the first instead of comparing every pair.

phased <- mark_phases(group_regulation_long, actor = "Actor", time = "Time",
                      n = 3, labels = c("early", "middle", "late"))
phases <- build_network(phased, method = "relative", actor = "Actor",
                        action = "Action", time = "Time", group = "phase")
over_time <- compare_networks(phases, reference = "early",
                              test = "permutation", iter = 1000, seed = 1,
                              actor = "Actor")
summary(over_time)
##             pair network_a network_b n_cells n_differing share_higher_a
##  early vs middle     early    middle      81          78           0.54
##    early vs late     early      late      81          77           0.49
##  share_higher_b mean_abs_diff max_abs_diff pearson spearman cosine jaccard
##            0.42          0.01         0.08    0.99     0.97   0.99    0.90
##            0.46          0.01         0.07    0.99     0.98   0.99    0.90
##                top_edge top_edge_higher n_sig_edges n_sig_nodes m_stat   m_p
##  synthesis -> consensus          middle           6           1   0.98 0.712
##       adapt -> cohesion            late           4           2   0.94 0.720
##  s_stat   s_p
##    0.08 0.546
##    0.07 0.673

The three phases are nearly identical: the edge weights correlate at 0.99 with those of the early phase, and the largest difference is 0.08. Neither global test is significant (p = 0.71 and 0.72 for M). Six and four of the 78 transitions differ at the 5% level, about the four that 78 tests at that level produce by chance; adjust = "BH" corrects the edge p-values for the number of tests.

plot(over_time, type = "edges", pair = "late")

pair selects the comparisons a view or a table shows, by the pair name, the two network names or one network name.
